name: Catherine of Aragon
role: Queen of England as Henry VIII's first wife (1509–1533); regent during the 1513 war with Scotland
summary: Spanish-born queen who was married to Henry VIII until the marriage was annulled by the English church in 1533. Her surviving words and her record show a devout Catholic who refused the royal supremacy, appealed her case toward Rome and governed England as regent in 1513. Little of her own writing sets out a general political programme.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: Catherine mobilised forces by issuing commissions of array in 1513. These wartime levies leave her position on keeping a standing military unresolved.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: Catherine defended Mary's status as a legitimate royal child and prepared her to exercise the governing authority of the Crown through dynastic succession.

abolish-legal-marriage.rationale: Catherine pursued formal legal recognition of her existing marriage through an appeal to Rome and continued to assert its binding legal status after the English annulment.

conscription.rationale: As regent Catherine commissioned Thomas Lovell to raise forces through county levies in 1513 and issued a warrant empowering him to punish obstruction of the levy.

dynastic-succession.rationale: Catherine prepared her daughter Mary to govern and resisted measures that would displace Mary as Henry’s legitimate child in the succession.

elective-rulers.rationale: Catherine prepared Mary to inherit the governing powers of the Crown as the legitimate child of Henry VIII and refused the oath to the revised succession.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: Catherine promoted an imperial alliance in 1520. Her intervention establishes her preferred partner at that moment, with no position on permanent military commitments.

national-law-over-international.rationale: Catherine appealed her annulment to the pope as the competent ecclesiastical authority. The appeal concerned church jurisdiction over marriage and leaves constitutional precedence over international law unresolved.

noblesse-oblige.rationale: Chapuys reports that Catherine customarily distributed alms to the poor at the Royal Maundy. The record establishes her own practice and leaves open whether she held that wealth itself creates a duty.

one-spouse-at-a-time.rationale: Catherine contested the English ruling that made Henry’s marriage to Anne lawful and maintained her claim to be his legal wife while their marriage stood in canon law.

separate-church-state.rationale: Catherine contested the loss of her public standing as queen by obtaining a ruling from the pope on the validity of her royal marriage and invoking it against the government's decision.

soldiers-refuse-war.rationale: Catherine used her regency powers to require levies for England’s war against Scotland and authorised punishment for obstruction of the muster.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Catherine challenged the jurisdiction of the legatine tribunal in her marriage case and sought a judgment from Rome. Her challenge concerned ecclesiastical jurisdiction and leaves the ruler's standing under England's civil laws unresolved.

state-harmful.rationale: As regent in 1513 Catherine exercised England's governing powers, including issuing military warrants and commissioning a judicial officer to hear criminal cases.

stay-neutral-between-blocs.rationale: In 1520 Catherine convened her council to oppose the planned meeting with Francis I and helped arrange Henry’s meetings with Emperor Charles V, which produced an agreement offsetting the French approach.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: Catherine appealed her marriage case to Rome and struck out the title that commissioners assigned her under the English judgment. She reserved the decision to the pope despite the king’s insistence that the English decision bound her.

notes: This pass checked diplomacy, regency and military administration, succession and courts, ecclesiastical jurisdiction, estate administration and poor relief, and household and educational patronage. The records document particular actions in those areas and give little evidence about general economic policy, civil liberties, ecology, technology, or modern international institutions. The disputed letter attributed to Catherine shortly before her death was not used.
